# Virtual Thread Scheduler

A runnable virtual thread needs an available carrier. This advanced example
occupies one carrier with a bounded CPU task, observes a queued virtual thread,
and changes the scheduler’s target parallelism at runtime. It uses
`VirtualThreadSchedulerMXBean`, a supported JDK-specific management API
available since JDK 24, with Java 25 as this module’s baseline. No preview
features are used.

Start with the introductory [Virtual Threads](../virtual-threads/README.md)
example. Here the lesson is scheduler capacity and progress, rather than task
creation or monitor pinning.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- distinguish target parallelism, carrier-pool size, mounted virtual threads,
  and queued virtual threads;
- observe how an occupied carrier can delay other runnable virtual threads;
- use `VirtualThreadSchedulerMXBean.setParallelism` to adjust scheduler capacity
  and restore its previous setting; and
- explain why increasing parallelism is a limited mitigation, rather than a
  throughput optimisation or a fairness guarantee.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25) JDK
or newer. This demonstration targets the HotSpot virtual-thread scheduler.
Ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to that JDK.

## The program to inspect

### An occupied carrier and queued work

The program runs in its own JVM with initial scheduler parallelism set to one.
The main thread is a platform thread, so it can manage the scheduler even when
the virtual-thread carrier is occupied. The occupier performs no blocking
operation and checks interruption and a ten-second deadline. `onSpinWait` is a
processor hint; it provides no coordination or visibility guarantee.

HotSpot does not time-slice virtual threads as described in JEP 444. With one
carrier occupied, the second virtual thread (the probe) can remain queued. A
bounded poll first observes a mounted thread; a 200 ms timed join then reports
whether the probe completed. These are diagnostic observations, not proof of
fairness, a JMM guarantee, or a performance measurement. Heavy system load or
different scheduler behaviour may prevent the intended sequence from appearing.

```text
target = 1:  carrier A -> occupier      probe queued
target = 2:  carrier A -> occupier      carrier B -> probe completes
```

The program reports whether the probe completed after adjustment while the
occupier was still alive. If that sequence was not observed, it says so rather
than presenting the run as evidence of recovery.

```java
final VirtualThreadSchedulerMXBean scheduler = scheduler();
final int originalParallelism = scheduler.getParallelism();
final Thread worker = Thread.ofVirtual().name("CARRIER-OCCUPIER").unstarted(Main::occupyCarrier);
final Thread probe = Thread.ofVirtual().name("QUEUED-PROBE").unstarted(() -> {});

try {
    scheduler.setParallelism(1);
    printScheduler("Target set to 1", scheduler);
    if (Thread.interrupted()) {
        throw new InterruptedException("Controller interrupted before starting work");
    }
    worker.start();
    awaitMountedWorker(scheduler, worker);
    probe.start();

    final boolean completedBefore = probe.join(Duration.ofMillis(200));
    printScheduler("Before adjustment", scheduler);
    log("Probe completed before adjustment: " + completedBefore);

    scheduler.setParallelism(2);
    final boolean completedAfter = probe.join(WAIT_LIMIT);
    final boolean workerStillRunning = worker.isAlive();
    printScheduler("After adjustment", scheduler);
    log("Probe completed after adjustment: " + completedAfter);
    log("Occupier still running at observation: " + workerStillRunning);
    if (completedBefore || !completedAfter || !workerStillRunning) {
        log("Starvation/recovery sequence was not observed in this run.");
    }
} finally {
    worker.interrupt();
    try {
        awaitTermination(worker, probe);
    } finally {
        scheduler.setParallelism(originalParallelism);
        printScheduler("Original target restored", scheduler);
    }
}
log("Both virtual threads terminated.");
```

### Read the measurements separately

`getParallelism()` reports the target. `getPoolSize()` reports carriers started
but not terminated, including idle carriers, and can exceed the target.
`getMountedVirtualThreadCount()` and `getQueuedVirtualThreadCount()` report
estimates, shown with `~` in the output. Counts may be unavailable (`-1`), and
the separately read values are not an atomic snapshot.

`setParallelism(2)` permits additional carrier capacity when needed; it does not
promise exactly two live carriers or immediate execution of the probe. Lowering
the target does not promise immediate termination of excess carriers. The
documented JDK target range is 1 to 32767. Unsupported schedulers may reject
adjustment with `UnsupportedOperationException`.

The scheduler belongs to the whole JVM. This example restores the original
target in `finally`, interrupts the cooperative occupier, and performs bounded
joins on both threads. It adds no executor or application synchroniser. A
successful join establishes termination; thread actions happen-before another
thread detects that termination. Timed joins that return `false` do not
establish that completion relationship. The MXBean counters do not publish task
results.

Increasing parallelism can allow queued work to progress when carriers are
occupied. It does not add CPU capacity, guarantee fairness, or solve arbitrary
deadlocks. Another occupied carrier can exhaust the extra capacity too. For
sustained CPU work, use an appropriate execution strategy; virtual threads are
intended chiefly for numerous tasks that spend much of their time blocked.
Diagnose the workload and its resource limits before changing a JVM-wide setting.

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from `examples/virtual-thread-scheduler` with Java 25 selected.
Use a fresh JVM so existing carriers and unrelated virtual-thread work do not
obscure the observation. Choose one execution path.

1. Compile and run using Maven. The exec configuration starts a separate JVM
   with `-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=1`.

   ```xml
   <plugin>
       <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
       <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
       <version>${maven-surefire-plugin.version}</version>
       <configuration>
           <useModulePath>false</useModulePath>
           <argLine>-Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=1</argLine>
       </configuration>
   </plugin>
   ```

   Run the example

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

   One observed run; scheduler counts and progress observations may vary.

   ```
   ...
   [12:34:56.789] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Virtual Thread scheduler
   [12:34:56.795] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Using Java 25.0.5.0.3
   [12:34:56.811] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Target set to 1: target=1, pool=1, mounted~=1, queued~=1
   [12:34:57.012] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Before adjustment: target=1, pool=1, mounted~=1, queued~=1
   [12:34:57.013] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Probe completed before adjustment: false
   [12:34:57.013] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] After adjustment: target=2, pool=2, mounted~=2, queued~=0
   [12:34:57.014] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Probe completed after adjustment: true
   [12:34:57.014] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Occupier still running at observation: true
   [12:34:57.014] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Original target restored: target=1, pool=2, mounted~=1, queued~=0
   [12:34:57.014] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Both virtual threads terminated.
   ...
   ```

2. Alternatively, build and test the executable JAR, then launch it explicitly
   with one initial carrier target. This property sets the initial target;
   the program changes it through the MXBean while running.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional *) Verify that the JAR file was created

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file

   ```
   ./target/libs
   └── virtual-thread-scheduler-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   Run the example

   ```shell
   java -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=1 \
     --module-path target/libs \
     --module demo
   ```

   One observed run; counts are implementation observations.

   ```
   [11:10:50.010] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Virtual Thread scheduler
   [11:10:50.014] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Using Java 25.0.5.0.3
   [11:10:50.027] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Target set to 1: target=1, pool=1, mounted~=1, queued~=1
   [11:10:50.228] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Before adjustment: target=1, pool=1, mounted~=1, queued~=1
   [11:10:50.229] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Probe completed before adjustment: false
   [11:10:50.229] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] After adjustment: target=2, pool=2, mounted~=2, queued~=0
   [11:10:50.229] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Probe completed after adjustment: true
   [11:10:50.229] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Occupier still running at observation: true
   [11:10:50.230] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Original target restored: target=1, pool=2, mounted~=1, queued~=0
   [11:10:50.230] [                                          Thread[#3,main,5,main]] Both virtual threads terminated.
   ```

Look for a delayed probe before adjustment, completion after adjustment, and an
occupier that was still alive at that observation. Read the target independently
from the pool size and estimates. The final lines confirm restoration and
termination. If the intended sequence is absent, do not infer a scheduler
guarantee from the output.

Tests assert bounded completion, thread termination, and restoration of a
non-default target on normal and interrupted paths. They do not assert a
particular scheduling sequence, carrier count, or latency.
